author: product-requirements-expert
title: Staff can cancel an upcoming visit from the owner's record
summary: The owner's record offers a cancel action beside each visit dated today or later; cancelling takes that visit off the pet's record outright, leaving nothing behind. A visit whose date has passed offers no cancel action and cannot be cancelled.
acceptance_criteria: Given a pet with a visit dated today or later, when the owner's record is opened, then a cancel action is offered beside that visit.
Given a pet with a visit dated before today, when the owner's record is opened, then no cancel action is offered beside that visit.
Given an upcoming visit, when it is cancelled, then the owner's record is shown again and that visit is no longer on the pet's record.
Given an owner with several pets and several visits, when one visit is cancelled, then every other visit of every pet is unchanged.
Given a cancel request for a visit dated before today, when it is submitted, then it is refused and the visit remains on the record.
Given a cancel request naming a visit that is not on the named pet's record, when it is submitted, then it is refused and nothing is removed.
Given a reader using a supported language, when the owner's record is opened, then the cancel action is worded in that language.
Edge case 3: a visit dated today is cancellable, although a visit dated today cannot be booked.
Edge case 4: cancelling the same visit twice is refused the second time.
Edge case 5: after a cancellation the pet's record is indistinguishable from one where the visit was never booked.
non_goals: A confirmation step between the cancel action and the removal
Retaining anything about a cancelled visit - cancelled state, cancellation log, or who cancelled (NG-10)
Cancelling a visit whose date has passed
Changing a booked visit's date or description (NG-5)
Deleting an owner or a pet (NG-4)
notes: Boundary check: this request reverses NG-4 (visits) and NG-5 (cancelling); both rows are narrowed in docs/prd.md rather than deleted, and each names REQ-VIS-010. The hard-removal question was decided, not escalated - rationale in docs/adr/2026-08-05-non-goal-cancelled-visit-retention.md, new row NG-10. Upcoming is deliberately wider than the booking rule: cancellable on the visit date itself, bookable only after it (PRD Visits edge case 3). The cancel label is user-facing wording, so REQ-LANG-002 requires it in all 11 message bundles; the existing I18nPropertiesSyncTest covers bundle parity, which is why no new test name asserts it. The ADR index table in docs/adr/README.md is outside this agent's write scope and still needs the new row - system-design-expert or doc-sync should add it.

author: system-design-expert
architectural_fit: Cancellation is the first removal path in this codebase, so it is new ground rather than an instance of an existing pattern. It stays inside the owner aggregate: Owner gains a cancellation method next to addVisit, Visit answers whether it is upcoming, and the existing OwnerRepository.save writes the removal - no new repository, no service layer, no new dependency. Two mechanics had to be ruled on rather than left to the inner loop, and both are recorded in docs/adr/2026-08-05-visit-cancellation-through-the-owner-aggregate.md with the current state in system-design.md (Contracts, Persistence, Threat Model). First, the pet-to-visit association declares no orphan removal today, so dropping a visit from the collection nulls its pet reference and leaves the row in place - invisible on the page, still in the database, contradicting NG-10 and edge case 5. Second, the cancel handler does not belong in VisitController, whose loadPetWithVisit model-attribute method runs before every handler in that class and attaches a blank visit to the loaded pet; saving that owner would cascade-persist an unfilled visit.
integration_points: Visit gains a predicate reporting whether it is upcoming - the visit date is today or later. It reads the current date the same way the Visit constructor already does; no Clock abstraction is introduced, because none exists in this codebase and adding one for a single predicate is novelty the pattern catalog does not sanction.

Owner gains a cancellation method taking the pet identifier and the visit identifier, sitting beside addVisit as the aggregate root's second write entry point. It resolves the pet, finds the visit on that pet, checks the visit is upcoming, removes it, and reports whether anything was removed. All three refusals the requirement names - pet not under this owner, visit not on that pet, visit already past - are decided here and return the same negative outcome. Cancelling twice is the not-found case on the second attempt, so edge case 4 needs no separate rule.
Pet's visits association declares orphan removal so the removed visit is deleted rather than orphaned with a null pet reference.

A new VisitCancellationController holds one POST handler under the existing nested route shape - owner, pet, visit identifiers, then the cancel action. POST rather than a link: the action destroys a record, and a safe method that mutates state is a pattern a demonstration application propagates. Not DELETE: no HTML form emits it and the hidden-method filter is not enabled. It loads the owner, delegates to the aggregate, and redirects back to the owner's record. It carries the same InitBinder id-disallow list as every other controller in the package.

Refusal and success are reported through the flash-attribute slots the owner detail template already renders - error and message. Refusal does not throw: the error page renders exception text, and a stale-page double submission is a routine outcome, not a fault.
ownerDetails.html renders the cancel control as a small inline form in each visit row, shown only when the visit is upcoming. The label resolves from the message bundle.

patterns.description: Owner.addVisit - the aggregate-root write entry point the cancellation method mirrors, including its identifier-resolution shape
processNewVisitForm - the mutate-then-save-then-redirect-with-flash shape the cancel handler follows
the per-visit row the cancel control is added to, and the error and message alert blocks at the top of the same template

Web controller row - no business rule in a controller, and the existing deviation does not extend to new rules. The upcoming check and the ownership check therefore live on Visit and Owner, not in the handler

risks.risk: A controller-level test cannot distinguish a deleted visit row from one orphaned with a null pet reference - both stop rendering. The requirement's edge case 5 and NG-10 are about the stored record, so the test names in the prd-entry alone leave the orphan case undetected.
risks.mitigation: Assert removal at the persistence level in ClinicServiceTests, which is already a DataJpaTest against the real schema - re-read after saving and assert the visit is gone, rather than asserting only what the page renders.

risks.risk: Orphan removal on a collection merged from a detached graph - the application disables open session in view, so save() merges a detached owner. If the mapping does not delete on merge, the feature silently orphans rows.
risks.mitigation: The persistence-level test above is the check. If it fails, the fallback is an explicit delete rather than weakening the aggregate boundary - see the ADR's rejected options before improvising.

risks.risk: The upcoming rule reads the current date, so a test whose fixture straddles midnight is flaky, and a visit dated today is cancellable while a visit dated today cannot be booked - the two boundaries deliberately differ by one day.
risks.mitigation: Build fixtures relative to the current date rather than from literals, and cover the today boundary explicitly - the prd-entry names theVisitDatedTodayShouldStillBeCancellable for exactly this.

risks.risk: Cancellation is the first route that destroys a record, on an application with no authentication and no CSRF protection. POST-only keeps it off safe methods but does not make it forgery-proof.
risks.mitigation: The demonstration baseline in security-principles governs: adding authentication or CSRF is NG-1 and out of scope, and this route is no weaker than the existing mutating routes. The threat model row in system-design.md now names cancellation as the destructive case so a reviewer sees it was ruled on, not overlooked.

notes: No design-doc-autofix records exist in the log; the autofix audit is a no-op for this dispatch. VOCABULARY: the domain term is Cancellation, and ubiquitous-language.md explicitly rejects Deletion and Removal as domain words and rejects the phrase cancelled visit - name the method, the route segment, the controller, the message keys, and the tests after cancellation; deletion vocabulary is admissible only for the persistence mechanic, which is what orphan removal is. TEST PLACEMENT: the prd-entry named VisitControllerTests.java as a test target, but the cancel handler does not live in VisitController (see architectural_fit), so its tests belong in a matching new test class - VisitControllerTests stays unchanged and the booking flow must keep passing untouched. OwnerRepository needs no change: findById and save already cover the path; it is listed in the prd-entry's file_targets and is expected to stay as it is. REQ-LANG-002: the cancel label needs a bundle key present in all 11 message files - I18nPropertiesSyncTest enforces key parity for the ten non-English bundles and separately fails on literal text in a template, so a hard-coded label fails the build. The refusal text takes a second key rather than a hard-coded English string: the existing hard-coded flash strings in the owner and pet controllers are a recorded deviation, and a new one is a fresh violation not covered by it. A success key is consistent with every other mutating flow here and is permitted; if added it comes from the bundle too. Resolving a bundle message inside a controller means injecting the message source through the constructor. docs/adr/README.md now indexes both 2026-08-05 ADRs - the requirements expert's non-goal ADR and the one written for this slice.

findings.description: The `@InitBinder setAllowedFields` method disallows binding of `id`/`*.id`, but `processVisitCancellation` takes only `@PathVariable int` parameters plus `Locale` and `RedirectAttributes` — none of which go through `WebDataBinder` property binding. In `VisitController` and `OwnerController` the same method guards a real `@ModelAttribute` command object; here it was copied without a binding target to guard, so it is dead code that misleads a future reader into thinking this handler accepts a bindable form object.
findings.fix: Remove the `@InitBinder setAllowedFields` method (and the now-unused `WebDataBinder`/`InitBinder` imports) from `VisitCancellationController` — there is no command object for it to protect.

Orphan removal on Pet.visits is precisely scoped and documented with a why-comment tying it to REQ-VIS-010

author: security-reviewer
approved_aspects: Authorization path is sound; no IDOR. VisitCancellationController binds ownerId/petId/visitId as primitive int path variables, loads the owner by id, and delegates to Owner.cancelVisit(petId, visitId). Owner.cancelVisit resolves the pet only through Owner.getPet(Integer), which iterates this owner's own pets, then matches the visit only within pet.getVisits() (a collection scoped by the pet_id join column). A request naming another owner's pet returns a null pet and refuses; a request naming a visit not on that pet finds no match and refuses. There is no path by which a supplied identifier reaches a repository lookup outside the loaded aggregate, so a forged identifier cannot cancel a visit under a different owner.

Refusal is a single collapsed negative outcome. All three refusals (pet not under this owner, visit not on that pet, visit not upcoming) return false and produce the identical flash message from key visitCancellationRefused, so the response is not an oracle distinguishing 'that visit exists but belongs to someone else' from 'no such visit'. Owner-id enumeration through the orElseThrow 500 page is unchanged from the existing OwnerController and PetController pattern, not introduced here.

The upcoming check is server-side, not merely a template concern. The th:if="${visit.upcoming}" guard only hides the control; Visit.isUpcoming() is re-evaluated inside Owner.cancelVisit's removeIf predicate, so a hand-crafted POST for a past visit is refused by the aggregate. No client-side-only authorization.

CSRF posture examined on its merits rather than accepted. The absence of a CSRF token is a real residual risk, but the design's reasoning holds for this codebase: with no authentication and no ambient credential, forgery grants an off-network attacker only what direct network reach already grants, and the pre-existing forgeable POST routes (/owners/new, /owners/{id}/edit, /pets/{petId}/edit, /visits/new) already permit irreversible overwriting of owner and pet data with no history or undo. Cancellation is therefore not a categorically new exposure class, only a new instance of an accepted one. POST-only genuinely earns its keep: it keeps the destructive action off safe methods, so no link, prefetch, or crawler can trigger it. Introducing a hand-rolled token without Spring Security (NG-1) would be false assurance in an application with no authenticated identity to bind the token to. The Threat Model row at docs/system-design.md:180 states the position accurately and without overclaim - it names cancellation as the one route that destroys a record and whose effect no other route can undo, and it reports 'None observed' for authentication, authorization, and CSRF rather than claiming the POST-only choice is a mitigation of forgery.

Redirect target is not attacker-controlled. 'redirect:/owners/{ownerId}' is expanded from the request's URI template variable, which is bound as a primitive int - no open redirect, no CRLF or header injection through the Location value.

Output escaping intact. Both flash slots the handler fills (message, error) are resolved from the message bundle rather than from request data, and ownerDetails.html renders them through th:text, which escapes. The new visit row cell and the cancel button label likewise use th:text. No th:utext, no inline unescaped output introduced.

Thymeleaf link preprocessing in the new form action (@{__${owner.id}__/pets/__${pet.id}__/visits/__${visit.id}__/cancel}) is not an expression-injection sink here: all three substituted values are Integer identifiers read from persisted entities, never user-supplied text. The pattern matches the adjacent pre-existing editPet and editVisit links in the same template.

Mass-assignment defense carried over: the new controller declares the same @InitBinder disallowing 'id' and '*.id' as every other controller in the package. The handler takes no form-bound command object at all, so its only inputs are three int path variables.

No injection surface added. Persistence goes through OwnerRepository.findById and save (Spring Data JPA); the cancellation itself is an in-memory collection removeIf. No string-concatenated query, no file path, no command execution, no deserialization entry point, and no reflection introduced.

Orphan removal reviewed for unintended destructive side effects, not only for the happy path. Adding orphanRemoval=true to Pet.visits makes any drop from that collection a row delete, so every existing path that merges an Owner was traced: PetController.updatePetDetails mutates the pet already attached to the freshly loaded owner rather than replacing it, VisitController adds to the collection, and Pet.visits is FetchType.EAGER so a merged pet always carries its loaded visits. No path was found that merges a Pet with an emptied or unloaded visits collection, so the new mapping cannot silently delete visit rows outside the cancellation flow.

Supply chain: no dependency or build change in the change set (build.gradle, settings.gradle, gradle.properties, and gradle/ are all untouched), so no new transitive surface and no CVE exposure is introduced by this slice. Change set scanned for hardcoded credentials across src/ and docs/ - no password, secret, token, api key, or credential literal added.

findings.description: testing-principles.md § Test Data Construction requires new tests (written from 2026-07-31 onward) to wrap production-type construction in factory methods rather than call constructors directly. All four new/newly-touched test classes for REQ-VIS-010 construct Owner, Pet, and/or Visit with raw `new Owner()`/`new Pet()`/`new Visit()` calls. VisitTests.java has no factory at all - every one of its four tests builds a Visit inline. OwnerTests.java and VisitCancellationControllerTests.java each have a `visit(id, date)` factory but still construct Owner and Pet directly. ClinicServiceTests.shouldDeleteTheRowOfACancelledVisit (a newly added test in an existing file) also constructs `new Visit()` directly - the pre-existing `new Visit()` at line 232 predates this slice and is not part of this finding. OwnerControllerTests.java is compliant: its new tests reuse the pre-existing george()/visit() factories.
findings.fix: Add createAnOwner(...)/createAPet(...) (or equivalent) factory methods to VisitTests, OwnerTests, and VisitCancellationControllerTests, and route the new ClinicServiceTests visit construction through a factory, per the brief's anonymous-factory pattern.

approved_aspects: The required persistence-level test (ClinicServiceTests.shouldDeleteTheRowOfACancelledVisit) is present and correctly distinguishes a deleted row from an orphaned one via a native COUNT query plus entityManager.clear() + reload, exactly as the design mandated - controller-level tests alone could not have caught an orphan-instead-of-delete regression
All seven test names named in the prd-entry are present and exercise the described behavior

The deliberate today-boundary asymmetry (cancellable today, not bookable today) is explicitly covered at both the unit level (VisitTests.theVisitDatedTodayShouldBeUpcoming) and the controller level (VisitCancellationControllerTests.theVisitDatedTodayShouldStillBeCancellable), with fixtures built relative to LocalDate.now() rather than literal dates, avoiding the midnight-flake risk the design called out

All PRD edge cases (3: today boundary, 4: double cancellation, 5: pet record indistinguishable from never-booked) have dedicated tests, and the three named refusal reasons (past visit, visit not on that pet, pet not under this owner) are each covered independently in OwnerTests at the unit level and duplicated at the controller level where relevant
AssertJ fluent assertions used throughout, no JUnit assertEquals/assertTrue found
Test data uses meaningful role-based constant names (UPCOMING_VISIT_ID, PAST_VISIT_ID, OTHER_PET_VISIT_ID, TODAY_VISIT_ID) with no mystery literals
./gradlew test and jacocoTestReport pass cleanly; Owner and Visit classes show 100% line coverage, VisitCancellationController 92%/100% line/branch, comfortably over the 80% brief target

OwnerRepository mocking in the two @WebMvcTest classes follows the codebase's existing, brief-tolerated controller-test convention (MockMvc as the sanctioned boundary mock, repository as a Mockito stub) and matches the sibling VisitControllerTests/OwnerControllerTests pattern already in the suite

summary: cancel an upcoming visit from the owner record

blast_radius.note: 26 files across 3 modules and 44 hunks, cross-stack: a JPA mapping change on the central aggregate, a new controller, the owner-detail template, eleven message bundles and four docs. It lands the codebase's first destructive route and its first removal path, on an app with no authentication and no CSRF (NG-1), so an unauthenticated POST now destroys a record no other route can restore - accepted and documented in the threat model, but new in kind.

semantic_surprise.note: The load-bearing line is one word - orphanRemoval = true on Pet.visits - which grants delete authority to every merge of the Owner graph, not just to cancellation. I traced each owners.save and saveAndFlush call site (OwnerController create and edit, PetController create and edit, VisitController booking, the new cancel handler): all bind onto an Owner loaded through a findById model attribute with EAGER visits, so no partial graph can silently delete rows today. The isUpcoming boundary - today counts as upcoming - is one day wider than the booking rule, deliberately, and matches the PRD edge case and the javadoc.

test_adequacy.note: Tests assert real outcomes, not the implementation: ClinicServiceTests.shouldDeleteTheRowOfACancelledVisit counts the stored row with a native query after entityManager.clear(), which is what caught the orphan-instead-of-delete bug (expected 0 but was 1), and no page-level assertion could have. Boundaries (yesterday, today, tomorrow, null date), all three refusals, double submission and cross-pet non-interference are each covered at unit and controller level. One narrow gap: the template's relative form action is asserted only as a substring while the controller test posts an absolute path, so template-to-mapping resolution is never exercised end to end - the adjacent editPet link uses the identical form.
